deep.reconstruction:
Gauss wrote this page in his interleaved copy of Christian Leiste's arithmetic textbook. The facing printed page (§97–98) explains the digit-by-digit square root algorithm and gives √2, √3, √5, √7 to about 8 places. It also notes that √8 = 2√2, √12 = 2√3, and so on.

The page is headed 'Einige berechnete Quadratwurzeln' ('some computed square roots'). It sets out a table, in two columns, of √n for exactly the squarefree integers 2 ≤ n ≤ 97:
2,3,5,6,7,10,11,13,14,15,17,19,21,22,23,26,29,30,31,33,34,35,37,38,39,41,42,43,46,47,51,53,55,57,58,59,61,62,65,66,67,69,70,71,73,74,77,78,79,82,83,85,86,87,89,91,93,94,95,97.
That is 60 entries. Every other non-square root reduces to these through √(k²m) = k√m, which is the rule the printed §98 illustrates.

The integer part of the root is written only where it changes:
- 1 at n=2
- 2 at 5
- 3 at 10
- 4 at 17
- 5 at 26
- 6 at 37
- 7 at 51, repeated at 55 at the head of the second column
- 8 at 65
- 9 at 82
These are exactly the first non-squares after 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81. The decimal digits follow the integer part.

Filled entries:
- √2 = 1.4142135623730950488017
- √3 = 1.7320508075688772935274
- √5 = 2.236067977499789696
- √6 = 2.4494897427831780981972840747059
- √7 = 2.6457513110645905905016157536(4.2)
- √10 = 3.16227766016837933199889354 4(.4)
- √11 = 3.31662479035539984911493273(6.4)
- √13 = 3.6055512754639
- √14 = 3.7416573867739(2)
- √15 = 3.8729833462074168
- √21 = 4.58257569495584000658805
- √41 = 6.403124237432848686488217(67)
- √65 = 8.062257748298549652367

A lighter repeated value '1.414213562373 +' (√2 again) stands near line 38. All other entries are blank; the table was left unfinished.

Several entries end in a final digit set off after a point ('…3544.4', '…736.4', '…364.2'). The same device appears on the next page for √1000. My interpretation is that it marks a fractional estimate of the next place, or the size of the remainder. It fits √10 (next digits …4|4327) but does not fit √11 or √7 cleanly.

No derivation is shown. The values were presumably obtained by the algorithm of §97 (digit-by-digit extraction, appending pairs of zeros) or by Newton/Heron division; this is my inference.

The next page continues the theme: √1000…√1008 to about 28 places, with seven orders of differences, i.e. a check by finite differences/interpolation. It then turns to arithmetic–geometric-mean series for the ellipse perimeter.
errors: √14: the page appears to end …677392, whereas √14 = 3.74165738677394138…; the 14th decimal should be 4 (possibly a slip or misreading of the hand).

√7: the true digits are …1615753639260…; the page ending '…1615753 64.2' is either a rounding to …75364 with an ambiguous appended '.2' (the true next-place fraction would be about −0.07), or a misread of the hand. Up to …161575363/4 the value is correct.

√11: the digits up to …4932736 are correct (true continuation …66707). The appended '.4' does not match the true next-place fraction (≈.67) under the 'next-digit' interpretation. The intended meaning of the appended figure is uncertain.
All other filled values (√2, √3, √5, √6, √10, √13, √15, √21, √41, √65) agree with the true values to the precision written, allowing truncation or rounding in the last place.

results.what: Table of square roots of all squarefree integers 2..97 (60 entries, partly filled) to 13–31 decimal places
results.modern_name: High-precision table of square roots of squarefree integers; reduction √(k²m)=k√m
results.usually_credited_to: Standard tabular practice (e.g. tables of Briggs, Vega, Lambert); routine

results.what: Values obtained (presumably) by digit-by-digit square-root extraction as in the printed §97
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient/medieval (Chinese, Indian, Arabic sources); textbook standard

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine youthful computational exercise in a school textbook. Its only notable features are the high precision (up to ~31 decimals) and the systematic choice of the squarefree n ≤ 97. Gauss's early taste for very long hand computation is well known.

checkable.asserts: gives 3.7416573867739413856, showing the page's final digit 2 (…677392) should be 4

checkable.sympy: [n for n in range(2,98) if all(n % (p*p) for p in range(2,10))]
checkable.asserts: reproduces exactly the 60 row labels of the table (squarefree n from 2 to 97)
